headline: Low water on the Danube uncovers sunken warships

sources.title: Low water levels: EU clears old Nazi warships from the Danube
WWII German Warships Reappear as Danube Drought Exposes Wrecks in Serbia
Danube WWII wrecks cleanup boosts Serbia economy, environment

chunks.text: The Danube has fallen so low this summer that a sunken German fleet has {{shown up}} again near Prahovo, a town in eastern Serbia. Photographs published in late July 2026 show rusted [[hulls]] {{sticking out}} of the water along a [[stretch]] that boats normally {{pass over}} without seeing anything. The ships have been down there since 1944. What is different this year is that crews are finally {{pulling them out}}.

chunks.text: In late 1944, the German navy was {{pulling back}} along the Danube as Soviet forces {{closed in}}. Rather than {{hand the ships over}} to the enemy, the crews sank about 200 of their own [[vessels]] near Prahovo, hoping the [[wrecks]] would block the river and {{hold up}} the Soviet [[advance]]. The plan lasted far longer than they [[intended]]. Eight decades later the hulls are still on the riverbed, and they have narrowed the safe [[channel]] from 180 meters to about 80.

chunks.text: That narrow channel costs Serbia about 5 million euros a year, because ships have to wait their turn to get through. Two boats passing each other can take anywhere from 40 minutes to four hours. [[Surveys]] with sonar and divers in 2021 {{turned up}} 38 wrecks in the worst section, and 21 of them are now being removed. The European Union {{put up}} a [[grant]] of 16.5 million euros through the Western Balkans Investment Framework, part of a project worth about 30 million. Divers {{clear away}} sand and silt with pumps before lifting gear takes each hull off the bottom. Some wrecks are too big or too [[fragile]] to move, so they are buried deeper instead, and others may still have [[ammunition]] on board.

chunks.text: The work is due to {{carry on}} until 2028. Serbia expects [[cargo]] on this part of the river to rise from 12.7 million tons a year in 2019 to 25 million by 2040, and one river ship can move as much grain as 120 trucks. Alessandro Bragonzi, who heads the European Investment Bank's office for the Western Balkans, said the project is an example of the kind of clean transport the bank wants to keep funding. In Prahovo, low water is an old story. The new part is that the ships people there {{grew up}} with may soon be gone [[for good]].
